frase_gancho.texto: The highest point, where the elite lived and governed.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue along your route: what comes next has to do with power and with the sky.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing at the spot where, according to several sources, the elite of Xochicalco lived and governed. The INAH explains that the Acropolis sits on a six-meter platform, west of the Main Plaza. It has buildings arranged around a central courtyard. Kenneth Hirth describes it as the ruler’s palace and the administrative center of the city. Medina Romero places it at the highest point of the site and mentions a temple-palace, workshops, storerooms, and offices. To the south, a four-meter wall with bastions and moats surrounds it. Think about how the city looks from here. The Main Plaza lies at your feet, to the east. Seeing and being seen were forms of power.

guion_largo.texto:
Climbing changes your perspective. This is the Acropolis.

According to the INAH, the Acropolis rises on a six-meter platform, west of the Main Plaza. It has several buildings arranged around a central courtyard. That layout resembles that of the Palace.

Kenneth Hirth describes it as the ruler’s palace and the administrative center of Xochicalco. Medina Romero goes in the same direction: he says it is the highest point of the site and that there was a temple-palace, workshops, storerooms, and administrative areas.

The INAH guide mentions it among the constructions of the Main Plaza and identifies it as the residence of the rulers. Andrews and Glascock add that the Acropolis had the main palace, four large storage spaces, and a temazcal. It is one of the two areas where the most weapons turned up, which suggests that the security of the elite was a priority.

Alvarado León describes it as the largest complex in the city by volume. Lucet adds something uncommon in Mesoamerica: a second floor was added to its tallest structure. To the south, the Acropolis is defended by a four-meter wall with bastions and moats, according to Medina Romero. A bastion is a part of the wall that juts out to keep watch and defend. A moat is a ditch. This means that the place where the rulers lived was also among the best protected.

Now think about the view. From a high place you can see who arrives and who climbs. The Main Plaza lies at your feet, to the east.

What we know for certain is modest: a platform, several buildings, and a defended city. The rest is filled in with imagination and with care.

texto: Look east and find the Main Plaza
Imagine whom the person who lived here saw arriving

texto.Platform height: six meters, according to the INAH
texto.Use: ruler’s palace and administrative center, according to Hirth
texto.Defense: four-meter wall with bastions and moats to the south, according to Medina Romero

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Acropolis was a temple.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The sources describe it as the residence and administrative center of the rulers, with workshops and storerooms.
